Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verses 1–3:

Surat al-Jinn is Meccan. [Narrated by Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Jinn was revealed in Mecca." See: al-Durr al-Manthur, 8/296.] In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

* *

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened⦆ They were nine, from the jinn of Nasibin. It is also said they were seven, who listened to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ). We have mentioned their report in Surat al-Ahqaf. ﴿Then they said⦆ when they returned to their people, ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an⦆. Ibn 'Abbas said: eloquent, meaning a Qur'an of wonder, which is marvelled at for its eloquence.

﴿It guides to righteousness⦆, calling to what is correct of tawhid (divine oneness) and faith. ﴿So we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord⦆. ﴿And that He, exalted is He, the majesty (jadd) of our Lord⦆. The people of Syria and Kufa, except Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, read "wa-annahu ta'ala" with a fatha on the hamza, and likewise what follows up to His words ﴿and that among us are the Muslims⦆. The others read them with a kasra. Abu Ja'far read "wa-annahu" with a fatha, which refers to what is conveyed as revelation, and a kasra for what is a report from the jinn.

The preferred reading is kasra throughout, because it is part of the speech of the jinn to their people, and so it is connected to their words: "So they said, indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an," and they said: "and that He, exalted is He."

Whoever reads with a fatha takes it as dependent on their words "so we have believed in it," and we believed in all of that; so he reads "anna" with a fatha because belief falls upon it.

﴿Jadd of our Lord⦆: the majesty (jalal) of our Lord and His greatness. This is said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. It is said: "jadda al-rajulu," meaning he became great; and from this is the saying of Anas: "When a man recited al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, he was great (jadda) among us," meaning his standing was elevated.

al-Suddi said: "jadd of our Lord" means the command of our Lord. al-Hasan said: the wealth (ghina) of our Lord. From this it is said of fortune: hazz (good fortune), and a man is majdud (fortunate).

Ibn 'Abbas said: the power of our Lord. al-Dahhak said: His action.

al-Qurazi said: His blessings and favours upon His creation.

al-Akhfash said: the kingdom of our Lord is exalted. ﴿He has not taken a consort, nor a son⦆. It is said: exalted is He, His majesty and greatness, above taking a consort or a son.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verses 4–6:**

﴿And that the foolish one among us⦆ means our ignorant one. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is Iblis. ﴿Against Allah an extravagance⦆ means a lie and transgression, and it is his attributing to Him a partner and a son.

﴿And that we thought⦆ means we supposed ﴿that humans and jinn would never speak⦆. Ya'qub read "taqawwala" (﴿they would speak⦆) with a fatha on the waw and a shaddah on it, ﴿against Allah a lie⦆. That is: we used to think they were truthful in their saying that Allah has a consort and a son, until we heard the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that there were men among humans who sought refuge with men among the jinn⦆. This was because a man among the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), when he travelled and nightfall overtook him in a barren land, would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the evil of the foolish ones of his people." He would then spend the night in safety and protection from them until morning.

Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shurayhi informed us, saying: Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, saying: Ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Abdullah ibn Yusuf ibn Ahmad ibn Malik narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim [Abd al-Rahman][[In "B" it is Abdullah, and the correct reading is what I have established.]] ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Marwazi narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Sa'id ibn al-Nu'man narrated to us in Tarsus, saying: Farwah ibn Abi al-Maghra' al-Kindi narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Malik narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq, from his father, from Kardam ibn Abi Sa'ib al-Ansari, who said: I went out with my father to Madinah on a certain need, and that was at the first time the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was mentioned in Makkah. Night overtook us at the dwelling of a shepherd of sheep. When midday came, a wolf arrived and seized a lamb from the sheep. The shepherd leapt up [and said][[In "B" it is "and called out."]]: "O Amir of the valley, your protection!" Then a caller we could not see called out, saying: "O Sirhan, release it!" So the lamb came running until it entered the flock, and the wolf had not wounded it at all.[[Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his tafsir (4/430), then commented: "This wolf which seized the lamb, being the young of the sheep, may have been a jinn, in order to frighten the human and make him afraid of it, then return it to him when he sought its protection, so as to mislead him, humiliate him and turn him away from his religion, and Allah knows best." It is attributed in al-Durr al-Manthur (8/298–299) to Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli in al-Du'afa', al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah, and Ibn Asakir. al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (7/129): "It was narrated by al-Tabarani, and in its chain is Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq al-Kufi, who is weak."]] Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) in Makkah: ﴿And that there were men among humans who sought refuge with men among the jinn, so they increased them in rahaq⦆, meaning: the humans increased the jinn in rahaq by their seeking refuge with their leaders.

Ibn Abbas said: "Sin (ithm)." Mujahid said: "Transgression (tughyan)." Muqatil said: "Error (ghayy)." al-Hasan said: "Evil (sharr)." Ibrahim said: "Pride (azamah)." This is because they would increase in transgression through this seeking of refuge, saying: "We have become masters over the jinn and the humans." The word "rahaq" in the speech of the Arabs means sin and committing what is forbidden.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verses 15–17:**

﴿And as for the deviators (al-qasitun), those who disbelieve, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ They were the fuel of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. Then He turned to the disbelievers of Makkah and said: ﴿And if they had remained upon the way (al-tariqah)...﴾ The scholars differed regarding its interpretation. Some people said: If they had remained upon the way of truth, faith and guidance, and thus been believers who obey, ﴿We would have given them abundant water (ma'an ghadaqa)﴾, meaning plentiful. Muqatil said: this was after He had withheld the rain from them for seven years.

Others said its meaning is: If they had been Muslims, We would have expanded [provision] for them in this world, given them much wealth and a pleasant, comfortable life. The striking of the abundant water as a parable is because all goodness and provision lie in rain, just as He said: "And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them..." to the end of the verse [al-Ma'idah: 66]. And He said: "And if the people of the towns had believed and been righteous, We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven..." to the end of the verse [al-A'raf: 96]. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that We may test them therein﴾, meaning: that We may test them as to how they give thanks for what they were granted. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Hasan.

Others said: its meaning is, "And if they had remained upon the way of disbelief and misguidance, We would have given them much wealth and expanded [provision] for them, so that We might test them therein," as a punishment for them and a gradual leading-on (istidraj), until they are beguiled by it and We then punish them. This is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Kalbi and Ibn Kaysan, as Allah said: "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of everything..." to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 44].

﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a severe punishment (adhaban sa'adan).﴾ The people of Kufa and Ya'qub read "yaslukhu" with a yā', while the others read it with a nūn, meaning: We shall cause him to enter. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Arduous (shaqqan)," and the meaning is one of hardship (dha sa'adin), i.e., of toil. Qatadah said: "There is no rest in it." Muqatil said: "There is no joy in it." al-Hasan said: "It only increases in severity." The root meaning of it is that climbing (al-su'ud) is hard upon [the people]. It is also narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the intended meaning of "the mosques" is the limbs upon which a person prostrates, and these are seven: the forehead, the two hands, the two knees, and the two feet. Abu Saʿid Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-ʿAbbas al-Humaydi informed us; Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Hafiz informed us; Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub informed us; ʿAli ibn al-Hasan al-Hilali and al-Sarri ibn Khuzaymah said: Yaʿla ibn Asad narrated to us; Wuhayb narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been commanded to prostrate upon seven limbs: the forehead" — and he pointed with his hand to it — "and the two hands, and the two knees, and the tips of the two feet, and not to tuck up garments or hair" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adhan, chapter on prostrating upon the nose: 2 / 297; and Muslim in al-Salat, chapter on the limbs of prostration and the prohibition of tucking up garments and hair and binding the hair in prayer, no. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 72, verse 24–28:

﴿Until, when they see that which they are promised﴾ meaning the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿then they will know﴾ at the descent of the punishment ﴿who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾: they or the believers.

﴿Say: I do not know﴾ [i.e., I do not know] [[Addition from "b".]] ﴿whether what you are promised is near﴾ meaning the punishment, and it is said the Resurrection, ﴿or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾ an appointed time and a limit whose duration will be long. Meaning: the knowledge of the time of the punishment is an unseen matter that none knows except Allah.

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ is in the nominative as an epithet of His saying "my Lord." It is also said: He is the Knower of the unseen. ﴿So He does not reveal﴾ does not inform ﴿His unseen to anyone,﴾ ﴿except whom He has chosen of a messenger﴾ except whom He chooses for His message, so He makes him aware of what He wills of the unseen, because he establishes the proof of his prophethood by the miraculous sign, by informing about the unseen. ﴿Indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ mentioning some directions as an indication of all of them. Rasadan means: He places before him and behind him guardians from among the angels who protect him from the devils, lest they eavesdrop, and from the jinn, lest they listen to the revelation and convey it to the soothsayers.

Muqatil and others said: Whenever Allah sent a messenger, Iblis would come to him in the form of an angel and inform him, so Allah would send from before him and behind him a guard of angels to protect him and drive away the devils. If a devil came to him in the form of an angel, they would inform him that he was a devil, so beware of him; and if an angel came to him, they would say to him: "This is the messenger of your Lord." [[See: al-Tabari: 29 / 122.]]

﴿That He may know﴾ Ya'qub recited "liyu'lama" with a dammah on the yaa', meaning: that people may know ﴿that﴾ the messengers ﴿have conveyed﴾. The others recited it with a fathah on the yaa', meaning: "that the Messenger may know" that the angels have conveyed ﴿the messages of their Lord.﴾ ﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾ meaning: Allah knows what is with the messengers, so nothing is hidden from Him. ﴿And He has enumerated everything in number.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He has counted what He created and knows the number of what He created, so the knowledge of nothing escapes Him, even the weight of an atom or a mustard seed. "Adadan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and if you wish, as an absolute object (masdar), meaning 'addan [[In "b" 'adadan.]].
